newsitem.title: GREECE: Research body warns of persistent Greek inflation.
newsitem.headline: Research body warns of persistent Greek inflation.

text.p: Greek inflation measured by consumer prices is unlikely to fall further under the present mix of economic policy and will close the year at 5.5 to 6.0 percent, the Foundation for Economic & Industrial Research (IOBE) forecast in its latest report.
Year-on-year inflation eased to 5.4 percent in May, the lowest for more than 20 years, but then edged up to 5.5 percent in June, compared with a European Union average of 1.5 percent in May.

The private research institute said in a report, "With signs of further easing of the EU inflation average in the coming months, we could witness divergence. Greece's inflation rate will very likely be stuck around 5.5 to 6.0 percent for many more months, hindering a further fall in interest rates."

Core inflation -- which does not include volatile prices for fuel, fruit and vegetables -- was running at 6.6 percent in May. Using the OECD definition of core inflation, which excludes all foodstuffs and not just fresh fruit and vegetables, that rate represents 7.6 percent annual price inflation. It eased to 7.0 percent in June.
To deal with a potential acceleration in inflation the IOBE called for more prudent incomes and fiscal policies, coupled with measures to strengthen competition.

"With the current policy mix unchanged it will be extremely difficult to see inflation improving by year-end. Our earlier forecast of 5.5 to 6.0 percent inflation by year-end 1997 still stands," it said.
Aggregate output, helped by a strong recovery in construction and agriculture and a mild improvement in tourism will result in GDP growth above 3.0 percent this year.
On monetary and foreign exchange policy, IOBE noted that market behaviour so far did not reflect concern about a potential drachma devaluation ahead.

But the "hard drachma policy" which has contributed to disinflation for a number of years, without much help from the other components of the government's policy mix, is nearing its limits, the report said.

Moreover, the country's current account deficit -- $853 million in February compared with $668 million in the same month a year earlier -- is expected to worsen this year against the backdrop of rising import penetration and deteriorating competitiveness.

"In the coming years, the balance of payments could prove to be a destabilising factor to the extent that a widening current account deficit continues to be the result of structural problems -- permanent market share losses in the domestic and foreign markets," IOBE said.

Another area of concern was the difficulty of stabilising the country's debt-to-GDP ratio, over 110 percent at the end of 1996, despite the continuous shrinking of the fiscal deficit in recent years. --George Georgiopoulos, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
